nodes.title: A debt furnisher's duties after a consumer disputes credit-report information through a credit bureau

derived_from.quoted_text: After receiving notice pursuant to section 1681i(a)(2) of this title of a dispute with regard to the completeness or accuracy of any information provided by a person to a consumer reporting agency, the person shall— (A) conduct an investigation with respect to the disputed information; (B) review all relevant information provided by the consumer reporting agency pursuant to section 1681i(a)(2) of this title; (C) report the results of the investigation to the consumer reporting agency; (D) if the investigation finds that the information is incomplete or inaccurate, report those results to all other consumer reporting agencies to which the person furnished the information and that compile and maintain files on consumers on a nationwide basis; and (E) if an item of information disputed by a consumer is found to be inaccurate or incomplete or cannot be verified after any reinvestigation under paragraph (1), for purposes of reporting to a consumer reporting agency only, as appropriate, based on the results of the reinvestigation promptly— (i) modify that item of information; (ii) delete that item of information; or (iii) permanently block the reporting of that item of information.

derived_from.quoted_text: A person shall complete all investigations, reviews, and reports required under paragraph (1) regarding information provided by the person to a consumer reporting agency, before the expiration of the period under section 1681i(a)(1) of this title within which the consumer reporting agency is required to complete actions required by that section regarding that information.

derived_from.quoted_text: Sections 1681n and 1681o of this title do not apply to any failure to comply with subsection (a) of this section, except as provided in section 1681s(c)(1)(B) of this title. Subsection (a) shall be enforced exclusively ... by the Federal agencies and officials and the State officials identified in section 1681s of this title.
derived_from.tier_rationale: Added 2026-08-30 (round 22) to encode the enforcement-exclusivity gap the corroboration pipeline's adversarial check found: subsection (a) duties (including the direct-to-furnisher dispute route this node already flagged as 'a separate duty under § 1681s-2(a)(8), not encoded') are enforceable ONLY by government regulators, not by a private consumer lawsuit -- unlike subsection (b), which does carry a private right of action. A consumer routed to '(a)(8) is a separate duty' without this caveat could wrongly believe a direct dispute to the furnisher preserved a private remedy. Confirmed via WebSearch cross-referencing Cornell LII and case commentary this session; direct web_fetch of this specific subsection was not independently re-verified against a live fetch this session -- flagged for the next live citation-check run rather than silently assumed.

derived_from.quoted_text: Though the word 'reasonable' does not appear in the statutory text of § 1681s-2(b), courts across circuits have read a reasonableness requirement into the furnisher's investigation duty. Courts have specifically rejected 'data conformity' review -- where a furnisher merely checks that its own internal database matches what it already reported, without examining supporting documents the consumer submitted -- as satisfying the duty. Some circuits (following the Fourth Circuit) now frame this as an 'objectively and readily verifiable' standard rather than a pure legal/factual distinction (see the legal_vs_factual_dispute_note below).
derived_from.tier_rationale: Added 2026-08-30 (round 22) -- this is case-law commentary, not a primary statutory or regulatory source, so tagged D per this schema's source-tier rule (corroboration only, not a sole anchor) rather than misrepresented as text of the statute itself. Confirmed via WebSearch of multiple law-firm and legal-publisher summaries this session (NCLC, Troutman Pepper, ABA Litigation Section); no single case is asserted as universally controlling since the specific standard (least-sophisticated/reasonable-consumer-style framing vs. the newer 'objectively and readily verifiable' test) varies by circuit and is actively evolving -- flagged as such in logic below rather than presented as settled uniform law.

logic.trigger: furnisher receives notice of a consumer dispute FORWARDED BY a consumer reporting agency (CRA) under § 1681i(a)(2) — this is distinct from a dispute sent directly to the furnisher (a separate duty under § 1681s-2(a)(8), not encoded in this node)
furnisher_duties_on_receiving_a_CRA-forw: review all relevant information the CRA provided
report investigation results back to the CRA
if inaccurate/incomplete: report that finding to every other nationwide CRA the furnisher furnished the information to
if inaccurate, incomplete, or unverifiable after reinvestigation: modify, delete, or permanently block that item for CRA-reporting purposes
logic.deadline: tied to the CRA's own § 1681i(a)(1) reinvestigation period — this node does not itself state that period's length (commonly cited as 30 days, extendable to 45 in some circumstances, but NOT independently verified against primary text this session; flagged rather than asserted)
logic.relationship_to_debt_collection: relevant when a debt collector or the original creditor is also furnishing information to credit bureaus about the disputed debt — a consumer disputing a debt's validity with the COLLECTOR under FDCPA §1692g (see FDCPA-VALIDATION-NOTICE-1692g) is a related but legally separate track from disputing the same debt's appearance on a CREDIT REPORT under FCRA (this node) — both may need to happen.
logic.reasonableness_standard_note: The statute's bare text ('investigate,' 'review all relevant information') does not itself say the investigation must be 'reasonable,' but courts have consistently read that requirement in. A furnisher that only re-checks its own internal records without examining supporting documents the consumer submitted (a 'data conformity' review) is generally NOT treated as having satisfied § 1681s-2(b) even though it technically 'investigated' and 'reported back' on time. This node's bare trigger/duties list, applied literally, would find such a furnisher compliant -- flagged here so that determination is not made without considering whether the investigation was substantive.
logic.practical_enforcement_note: The direct-dispute route flagged elsewhere in this node ('a separate duty under § 1681s-2(a)(8), not encoded in this node') is NOT privately enforceable -- § 1681s-2(c)-(d) commits subsection (a) enforcement exclusively to federal/state regulators, unlike subsection (b), which does carry a private right of action. Practically, a consumer who wants a private FCRA remedy against a furnisher needs to dispute through a CRA (triggering subsection (b)), not directly with the furnisher alone.
logic.legal_vs_factual_dispute_note: Some circuits have held a furnisher has no § 1681s-2(b) duty to resolve purely LEGAL disputes (e.g., whether a debt buyer legally owns the debt, or whether it is time-barred) as opposed to FACTUAL inaccuracies (e.g., wrong balance, wrong dates) -- only a court can finally resolve legal validity questions. Other, more recent circuit decisions have moved away from that legal/factual line toward an 'objectively and readily verifiable' test, under which even some legal-sounding disputes can trigger a duty if they are readily checkable. This is a genuinely unsettled, circuit-dependent question this node does not resolve -- flagged rather than asserted either way.

drafting_revisions.summary: Added the enforcement-exclusivity caveat for the (a)(8) direct-dispute route (not privately enforceable), the reasonable-investigation judicial gloss (rejects mere records-parroting), and the legal-vs-factual dispute distinction (flagged as genuinely unsettled/circuit-dependent rather than asserted as a clean rule); added 2 checklist items.

completeness_checklist.fact: Whether the consumer disputed the item directly with a credit bureau (CRA) — triggers this node — versus disputing directly with the furnisher/collector (a different provision, not encoded here)
Date the CRA notified the furnisher of the dispute
Whether the furnisher reported back to the CRA within the applicable reinvestigation window (window length not encoded in this node — flagged gap)
What the furnisher's investigation concluded, and whether it modified/deleted/blocked the item accordingly if inaccurate/incomplete/unverifiable

Whether the furnisher's investigation went beyond checking its own internal records to actually reviewing supporting documents the consumer submitted with the CRA dispute (a bare records-check is widely treated as an unreasonable/inadequate investigation)

Whether the consumer's dispute is a factual claim (wrong amount, wrong dates, mistaken identity) or a legal claim about the debt's validity/ownership/enforceability (e.g., statute of limitations, chain of title) -- courts differ, by circuit, on whether the latter triggers a furnisher duty at all

consequences_and_next_steps.action: If disputing a debt's appearance on a credit report, dispute directly with the credit bureau (CRA), not just the collector — this triggers the CRA-forwarded-dispute duty encoded here, which the collector-only validation-dispute route (FDCPA §1692g) does not.

If the furnisher fails to investigate, fails to report back, or continues reporting inaccurate information after a reinvestigation should have caught it, that is a potential independent FCRA violation.
